claims.claim: The HIPAA rules apply to health plans, health care clearinghouses, and health care providers who transmit health information in electronic form in connection with a covered transaction, and, where specified, to business associates - so an organization is not covered merely because it holds health information.

A business associate is a person or organization outside a covered entity's workforce that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits protected health information on the entity's behalf, or provides listed services involving disclosure of it; subcontractors are included.

Protected health information excludes education records covered by FERPA, records described at 20 U.S.C. 1232g(a)(4)(B)(iv), employment records held by a covered entity as employer, and information about a person deceased more than 50 years.

HIPAA does not preempt a state privacy law that is more stringent, where 'more stringent' includes restricting a use or disclosure HIPAA would permit or giving the individual greater rights or more information.

The minimum necessary standard requires reasonable efforts to limit protected health information to the minimum needed for the purpose of a use, disclosure, or request, and does not apply to disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment, disclosures to the individual, uses under an authorization, disclosures to the Secretary, or uses required by law.

A covered entity may use or disclose protected health information for its own treatment, payment, and health care operations, and may disclose it to another health care provider for that provider's treatment activities, without a signed authorization.

A valid HIPAA authorization must contain specified core elements - a specific and meaningful description of the information, who may disclose, who may receive, each purpose, an expiration date or event, and the individual's signature and date - plus statements about revocation, conditioning, and the potential for redisclosure; it must be in plain language and the individual must receive a copy.

HIPAA permits, but does not require, a covered entity to disclose protected health information in good faith when it believes disclosure necessary to prevent or lessen a serious and imminent threat to health or safety, to a person reasonably able to prevent or lessen the threat; it also distinguishes a court order (disclose only what the order expressly authorizes) from a bare subpoena (which requires satisfactory assurances about notice or a qualified protective order).

42 CFR Part 2 protects records that would identify a patient as having or having had a substance use disorder and that were obtained by a federally assisted substance use disorder program; the protection is program-based rather than diagnosis-based, and federal assistance is defined broadly to include Medicare participation, controlled-substance registration for this treatment, federal funds in any form, and tax-exempt status.

Under Part 2, the restrictions apply regardless of whether the requester already has the information, is a law enforcement official, or holds a subpoena; Part 2 records and testimony relaying their content may not be used against the patient in civil, criminal, administrative, or legislative proceedings without specific written consent or a qualifying court order under subpart E, and a consent for that purpose may not be combined with any other consent.

The 2024 final rule at 89 FR 12472 implemented section 3221 of the CARES Act, was effective April 16, 2024 with a compliance date of February 16, 2026, and aligned Part 2 more closely with HIPAA - permitting a single written consent for all future treatment, payment, and health care operations disclosures, allowing recipients that are covered entities or business associates to redisclose under HIPAA without segregating records, applying HIPAA breach notification, and applying HIPAA civil and criminal penalty provisions.

Part 2 does not preempt stricter state law, and no state law may authorize or compel a disclosure Part 2 prohibits; Part 2 also does not bar reporting suspected child abuse and neglect to state authorities, though the underlying records remain protected.

Under Part 2, consent authority for a minor follows state consent-to-treatment law: where a minor may lawfully obtain substance use disorder treatment alone, only the minor may consent to disclosure, including disclosure to a parent for reimbursement; where state law requires parental consent to treatment, both the minor and the parent or guardian must sign.

The federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act requires states to have provisions requiring certain individuals to report known or suspected child abuse and neglect; as of the Child Welfare Information Gateway review current through May 2023, approximately 46 states plus the District of Columbia and several territories enumerate mandated professions (social workers in 41 states), Indiana, New Jersey, North Carolina, and Wyoming require all persons to report without enumerating professions, and approximately 17 states plus Puerto Rico impose a duty on any person.

The reporting trigger is typically suspicion or reasonable belief formed in the reporter's official capacity, and the reporter must report the facts producing the suspicion rather than proof; most states and territories restrict privileged communications for mandated reporters, with physician-patient and spousal privileges most commonly denied and attorney-client most commonly affirmed.

Duty-to-protect obligations are state-law doctrines rather than a single national rule: the 1974 Tarasoff decision framed a duty to warn a foreseeable victim and the 1976 rehearing framed a broader duty to exercise reasonable care to protect; a 2014 review summarizing Edwards's 2012 classification counted 23 states with a mandatory duty in statute, 10 with a mandatory duty in common law, 11 permitting disclosure without requiring it, and 6 with no statutory or case-law guidance, and reported a survey in which 76 percent of psychologists misidentified their own state's duty-to-protect law.

In Jaffee v. Redmond, 518 U.S. 1 (1996), the Supreme Court recognized a psychotherapist-patient privilege under Federal Rule of Evidence 501 and held that the reasoning extended to licensed clinical social workers, while declining to define the privilege's full contours and acknowledging that exceptions may exist, including where disclosure is the only way to avert a serious threat of harm.

FERPA governs education records; rights transfer to the student at 18 or upon enrolling in a postsecondary institution, and records made by a professional acting in that capacity, used only in connection with treatment, and disclosed only to those providing the treatment are excluded from education records - an exclusion that ends if the record is disclosed to anyone else.

The NASW Code of Ethics (2021) directs social workers to discuss the nature and limits of confidentiality with clients as soon as possible in the relationship and as needed thereafter; to disclose only the minimum necessary when preventing serious, foreseeable, and imminent harm; to seek agreement among participants in family, couples, and group counseling while informing them that the worker cannot guarantee all participants will honor it; and to protect confidentiality in electronic communication, record storage, and consultation with colleagues.

Part 2 programs must give patients notice at admission that federal law protects these records and a plain-language notice of privacy practices no later than first service delivery, and must maintain written security policies covering paper and electronic records; HIPAA breach notification requirements now apply to them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many states impose a mandatory duty to warn or protect
positions: Johnson, Persad, and Sisti (2014), summarizing Edwards's 2012 classification: 23 mandatory by statute, 10 mandatory by common law, 11 permissive, 6 with no guidance.
Various secondary summaries circulating online report different totals, most commonly '29 mandatory / 17 permissive' or similar, without a stated classification method or date.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses only the peer-reviewed 2014 review's figures, labels them as a 2012 classification summarized in 2014, and states explicitly that the reader must check their own jurisdiction. Unsourced aggregate counts were not used.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the 42 CFR Part 2 2024 rule is currently in force and enforced
positions: The rule text at 89 FR 12472 states an effective date of April 16, 2024 and a compliance date of February 16, 2026.
Secondary reporting describes an HHS Office for Civil Rights enforcement announcement in February 2026.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Only the dates stated in the Federal Register document itself and the amendment notes carried in the current eCFR text are asserted. The secondary reporting about an enforcement announcement was not used, because hhs.gov was not directly reachable for verification during research.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Status of the 2024 HIPAA reproductive health care privacy provisions, which still appear in the current eCFR text of 45 CFR 164.502(a)(5)(iii) and 164.512(c)(3)
positions: The provisions remain in the codified regulation text.
Their enforceability has been the subject of litigation reported after promulgation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Excluded from the lesson entirely and recorded as out of scope. The topic could be taught fully without them, and asserting either position would have required legal analysis this lesson should not perform.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted that 'Confidentiality And Privacy is a foundational concept' and offered no factual content whatsoever; nothing in it was verifiable because nothing in it was substantive.

The draft treated confidentiality and privacy as a single undifferentiated concept, which the research contradicts: privacy, confidentiality, and privilege are separately defined and separately enforced.
The draft's three quiz items tested generic study skills rather than any content in this topic and cited no sources.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft; no sentence of it survives.
Separated privacy, confidentiality, and privilege, and made the distinction a Compare/Contrast item because students routinely merge them.
Stated HIPAA's actual scope from 45 CFR 160.102 and 160.103 and made the belief that HIPAA covers all holders of health information an explicit Common Mistake.
Framed duty to protect as a set of state-law doctrines with counted variation rather than as a single national Tarasoff rule, and distinguished the 1974 duty to warn from the 1976 duty to protect.
Added the 42 CFR Part 2 regime, verified the 2024 rule's Federal Register citation, effective date, and February 16, 2026 compliance date against the rule document itself.
Distinguished a subpoena from a court order under both HIPAA and Part 2.

Added an explicit statement in the lesson body, key takeaway, and provenance that this is educational material and not legal advice, that federal law described is U.S. federal law, and that state law varies and is frequently stricter.
Added cross-references to ethics-in-helping-professions and professional-boundaries so codes, values, decision-making models, and dual relationships are not duplicated here.
rightsIssues: U.S. federal regulations and Federal Register documents are edicts of government and are not subject to copyright; even so, no regulatory prose was reproduced beyond short defined terms and section numbers.
The NASW Code of Ethics is copyrighted. It is recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY; its standards are described in original wording and no sentence of it is quoted or closely paraphrased.

The JAAPL review article and the Cornell LII reproduction of the Supreme Court opinion are recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY; findings and holdings are stated in original wording. The underlying Supreme Court opinion is itself a government edict, but the LII presentation carries site material, so the record is kept conservative.
The Child Welfare Information Gateway publication is a U.S. federal government work; its counts are cited as data with the publication's 'current through May 2023' date attached.
